content.text: left/right keys don't work in terminal switcher, but they do work in workroom switcher

input.prompt:
In this macOS SwiftUI codebase (workroom app, under macapp/), find the "terminal switcher" and "workroom switcher" UI components/views. Bug report: left/right arrow keys don't work in the terminal switcher, but DO work in the workroom switcher.

I need you to:
1. Locate both switcher views/components (search for "switcher", "TerminalSwitcher", "WorkroomSwitcher", or similar names).
2. For each, find how left/right arrow key handling is wired up — look for `onKeyPress`, `.keyboardShortcut`, NSEvent local monitors, `isAppShortcut`, or any keyDown handling.
3. Identify concretely why the workroom switcher's left/right arrow handling works but the terminal switcher's doesn't. Consider: is the terminal switcher rendered while a Ghostty terminal surface has focus (which might swallow/consume arrow keys before SwiftUI sees them)? Is there a difference in how each switcher captures focus vs the underlying terminal view?
4. Report file paths and line numbers for all relevant code (switcher views, key handling, focus state, any NSEvent monitors like AppDelegate's cmd-key monitor, and GhosttySurfaceView's `isAppShortcut`).

There's a known related pattern in this codebase: keyboard shortcuts must be registered in `GhosttySurfaceView.isAppShortcut` or a focused terminal (libghostty) will swallow the keystroke before SwiftUI ever sees it. Check if arrow keys are handled there or if that's relevant to left/right specifically for a "switcher" overlay.

Report back file:line references and a clear explanation of the root cause difference between the two switchers. This is a read-only investigation — do not make any edits.

100	/// caller's `.background(tokens.panel.ignoresSafeArea())`, SwiftUI also paints behind the (transparent,
101	/// full-size-content) title bar, so the themed colour holds even between notifications.
102	private struct SettingsWindowThemer: NSViewRepresentable {
103	  func makeNSView(context: Context) -> NSView {
104	    let probe = NSView(frame: .zero)
105	    context.coordinator.attach(to: probe)

107	  }
108	
109	  func updateNSView(_ nsView: NSView, context: Context) {

115	  final class Coordinator {
116	    private var observers: [NSObjectProtocol] = []
117	    private weak var probe: NSView?
118	
119	    func attach(to probe: NSView) {
120	      self.probe = probe
121	      DispatchQueue.main.async { [weak self] in Self.applyToProbe(self?.probe) }
122	
123	      let center = NotificationCenter.default
124	      // Theme switch: re-apply regardless of which window posted it.
125	      observers.append(
126	        center.addObserver(forName: .themeDidChange, object: nil, queue: .main) { [weak self] _ in
127	          MainActor.assumeIsolated { Self.applyToProbe(self?.probe) }
128	        })
129	      // Window lifecycle events that reset the titlebar/background on a static view. Filtered to our
130	      // own window in the handler.
131	      for name: NSNotification.Name in [
132	        NSWindow.didUpdateNotification,
133	        NSWindow.didBecomeMainNotification, NSWindow.didResignMainNotification,
134	        NSWindow.didBecomeKeyNotification, NSWindow.didResignKeyNotification,
135	        NSWindow.didResizeNotification,
136	      ] {
137	        observers.append(
138	          center.addObserver(forName: name, object: nil, queue: .main) { [weak self] note in
139	            MainActor.assumeIsolated {
140	              guard let window = self?.probe?.window,
141	                (note.object as? NSWindow) === window
142	              else { return }
143	              SettingsWindowThemer.apply(to: window)
144	            }
145	          })
146	      }

149	    @MainActor private static func applyToProbe(_ probe: NSView?) {
150	      SettingsWindowThemer.apply(to: probe?.window)
151	    }

153	    deinit {
154	      observers.forEach(NotificationCenter.default.removeObserver)
155	    }
156	  }

158	  // Guarded so each notification only writes when something actually reset — no relayout churn.
159	  @MainActor static func apply(to window: NSWindow?) {
160	    guard let window else { return }

questions.question: Root cause confirmed: macOS Mission Control's stock "Move left/right a space" shortcut (⌃←/⌃→, enabled by default on a fresh Mac) grabs those keys before Workroom's event monitor ever sees them — same class of OS-level collision already documented for ⌥Tab vs AltTab/HyperSwitch, but that one is opt-in software; this one ships ON by default for basically everyone. Fixing it needs a decision on scope: just expose the existing (currently UI-less) retune preference, or also change the pane switcher's default trigger so it works out of the box?

options.label: Settings picker only
options.description: Add a Settings UI for the already-existing switcherPaneModifier/switcherWorkroomModifier preference (the code comment says 'no Settings UI yet' — this is the documented escape hatch). Keeps ⌃Tab as the default pane-switcher trigger, so most users still hit the OS collision until they find the new setting and retune it themselves.

options.label: Change default + add picker (recommended)
options.description: Same picker, but also change the pane switcher's default trigger away from Control (e.g. to ⌃⌘) so arrows work out of the box for everyone, not just users who discover the setting. Tradeoff: ⌃Tab stops opening the pane switcher by default — a visible muscle-memory change for existing users, who'd need to retune back to ⌃Tab via the new picker if they prefer it.
